utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, Mark Harmon, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. And for the Defence, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Perisic will be represented in the courtroom today by Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith, Boris Zorko, and Mr. Chad Mair today with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Once again, may the record show that the Chamber is still sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the absence of Judge Picard. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Again, I'll still remind you, Mr. Simic, that you are bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, nothing else but the truth. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Simic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If perhaps the binders that were made available to the witness yesterday could be made available to him again. And there should be a binder that is marked "65 ter," and it's that particular binder that I'd like him to look at. And if we could please see Prosecution 65 ter 2022 on the screen, 2022. And there should be a tab in that binder referring to 2022.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, this document presents the first issue with regard to the question of fresh evidence, if this is not a P exhibit but a 65 ter exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I've read the jurisprudence, fresh evidence -- fresh evidence addresses, if I could pull it out -- I do stand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Corrected?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I do stand corrected, Your Honour. Mr. Guy-Smith is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought so too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. And if I could have one more moment, please. Well, quite frankly, Your Honour -- Your Honour, quite frankly, I'm not sure that Mr. Guy-Smith is correct, and I will explain why. If I direct your attention to the language from our Appeals Chamber, the 26th of February, 2009, in the case of Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic and all, and this was a decision on an interlocutory appeal regarding presentation by the Prosecution of documents during its cross-examination of Defence witnesses, and paragraph 15 of that decision says the following: "With regard to fresh evidence, this refers to material that was not included in the Prosecution Rule 65 ter list and not admitted during the Prosecution's case in chief, but that is tendered by the Prosecution when cross-examining Defence witnesses." I read that, Your Honour, as conjunctive, as a conjunctive definition, material that was not included in the Prosecution's 65 ter list and not admitted during the Prosecution's case in chief. The document -- may I finish, please? The document that I wish to show the witness now is a document that was on the Prosecution's 65 ter list, and that is where I part company with Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I think there's a good --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there certainly is a good reason why we part company, inasmuch as Mr. Saxon has indicated this is a conjunctive as opposed to disjunctive reading of the situation, and that is, in large measure, based upon the Trial Chamber's decision in the very case in which Mr. Saxon is discussing the appeal. And I'm referring now to the decision of the Trial Chamber of the 27th of November, 2008, in which it's really quite clear that the Prosecution took the position, in paragraph 13, and I quote: "The Prosecution further relies on Rule 90(H) of the Rules in order to justify the presentation and cross-examination of 'new documents.'" Which is what we're referring to here, also using the term "fresh evidence." And then there's a parenthetical remark which I think directly contradicts the position that Mr. Saxon's taken here and directly contradicts the position that the Prosecution took there, which is: "In other words, documents that have not yet been admitted." Which go to the proof of the guilt of the accused, which is -- we'll get to that of this particular analysis. But with regard to the issue of whether this a conjunctive or disjunctive analysis, I think it is quite clear that with regard to the appeal decision that was relied upon, the Prosecution took a disjunctive as opposed to a conjunctive position. And so that internally, if one is to view what the analysis is of the Appeals Chamber, it's quite clear that they were relying on the Prosecution's assertion that they were dealing with documents that have not yet been admitted, which is precisely the kind of document that Mr. Saxon is presently intending on using.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that had been the intention of the -- of our Appeals Chamber, then I would think, then, they would have written that sentence in paragraph 15 much more differently. They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I tend to disagree, Your Honour. And I think that now what is happening is that Mr. Saxon is substituting his desire for whether or not something is to be conjunctively or disjunctively understood for what the reading is. And it becomes a question of the plain reading of the sentence. And if it has two interpretations, which I don't believe it does, based upon the history of the litigation in question, then that poses another dilemma and something that perhaps the Appeals Chamber may have to take care of in the future. But in the history of this particular litigation, I don't think there's any question at all that this was disjunctive analysis based upon a disjunctive presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I've looked at the decision of the 26th of February, 2009, which I have here before me. But I have not had the benefit of the one of the 27th of November, 2008, which is, I think, the first-instance decision that was being appealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. So that's the decision upon which the Appeals Chamber is making a determination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- of the evidence that's been presented and the definitions that the parties took with regard to that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So with the definition that the parties took with regard to the evidence would then be resolved by the determination of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely, without a doubt. But since we're dealing with an issue of whether or not something's to be read as disjunctive of conjunctive, and we're dealing now with an issue of pleading. Since in the first-instance the Prosecution took the disjunctive position, I don't believe it's appropriate for the Prosecution here to be interpreting the Court of Appeal's decision to be anything other than that which they proffered in the first instance, because the concerns were, in large measure, dealing not with the question of a 65 ter list, but the question of what are the principles that surround the issue of the requirements of the Prosecution with regard to the evidence they present in their case in chief. That's the underlying thrust of this. I think you also may well be familiar with this in your own experience, having sat on another case where this issue came up as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think it happened in the Delic case at some point as well. But the fact of the matter is that the 65 ter issue is, in many senses, a secondary issue to the underlying question that is been presented in this part of -- in this litigation. Now, it does factor into part of the analysis, but I don't think we've gotten to that point yet, in terms of the presentation that Mr. Saxon has made. Mr. Saxon is taking the position that 65 ter documents are necessarily excluded from this analysis, which I believe is not a reasonable or an accurate interpretation, predicated upon the state of the decision and the law that we have at the present time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, if my understanding of the Appeals Chamber's decision, particularly in their decision of the 15th of April, 2008, in the Delic matter, the considerations that I think are enunciated there center around fair trial for an accused, proper notice, time to prepare, and all those considerations. And could it clearly be said that a document that was on the 65 ter list but which was not tendered during the evidence-in-chief of the Prosecution, that the Defence has proper notice of it at this stage? Obviously, when it was not used in the case in chief, they must have disregarded it. And when it now gets tendered, they need to get proper notice of it and have sufficient time to prepare for it. I think this is the underlying thinking of the Appeals Chamber in its decision. Really, the question of listing one's 65 ter list doesn't seem to be me to be certainly an important issue. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will agree with you in part, Your Honour, but not completely, and here is why. And eventually we may have to ask the witness to leave the courtroom, but I'll try to -- perhaps it would be appropriate at this point to ask the witness to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you excuse us for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I don't agree with Your Honour's position completely, because I think there may be circumstances, and I think where we are at this moment is one of them, where it is certainly not unfair to the Defence for the Prosecution to use and possibly seek the admission of at document from its 65 ter exhibit list that it did not tender during its case in chief. And here's why, in this situation, in fact, the Prosecution believes it would be unfair to the Prosecution if the Prosecution were prohibited from doing this. Right now, I'm cross-examining this witness about the so-called Drina Plan, which obviously is a major part of this witness's evidence. It's an important document in the Prosecution's case. And for the first time on Wednesday afternoon, the Prosecution was informed that the Defence position about the Drina Plan is that this was a work of so-called strategic camouflage, and it seems to me -- and, you know, the Prosecution was not informed about this in the Defence pre-trial brief, et cetera, et cetera, not until Wednesday. And suddenly the -- certainly, if this was going to be part of the defence of General Perisic, the Defence would understand that the Prosecution, to test that position, might want to use any document related to the Drina Plan. And in this case, we have one document - it's related to the series of documents that I was showing the witness yesterday - that was not admitted into evidence, but it was on our 65 ter list. And I don't think it should be a matter of any surprise, then, to the Defence, given the situation that we're in, that the Prosecution would want to use this evidence, particularly since it's material that was disclosed years ago to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at what Mr. Saxon has just said, I think it's curious and strange, in the first instance, that if this document is as important as Mr. Saxon now claims it to be, that this was not a document that was presented in the Prosecution's case in chief with regard to a whole series of documents that were presented with regard to the very thing we're discussing here, which is the Drina Plan. So I'm not sure that the argument, as it's presently put forth to Your Honours, really holds water, because, in fact, what it seems to be being said by Mr. Saxon is that, Since the Defence has challenged Prosecution evidence, we now are in a position to rebut that challenge, which is a different standard to be used than the standard that Mr. Saxon is presently dealing with. And I think part of the difficulty that we're having here is that the underlying principle, that the Prosecution is supposed to present that evidence and those exhibits in their case in chief to establish their case, and obviously their position, which is the guilt of the accused, is to be done at that time; isn't to be done piecemeal, isn't to be done through cross-examination with fresh evidence, and in a situation whereas here, from the Prosecution we have been told this an important document concerning an important matter, which is part of -- I think probably one of the foundation principles of their case, their failure to have presented that document to the Chamber in their case in chief is perhaps unfortunate and perhaps an oversight, or perhaps it's sandbagging and they're relying on weight. I'm not in a position to say. But you have seen myriad documents with regard to the Drina Plan, you've seen myriad documents of this sort in their case in chief. At this point, to single out this one particular document as now having this critical significance, where they full well know what case their prosecuting and they full know well that we're challenging their evidence, I don't think is appropriate under the decisional law as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. The issue that Your Honour raised was whether 65 ter documents are automatically included in this concept of fresh evidence, first from the Delic appeal decision, where it is not specifically stated there, and then from the subsequent Prlic appeal decision, where, again, from a fair reading, it would seem to exclude documents; it would not include documents that were on the Prosecution's 65 ter list from this world or universe of so-called fresh evidence. That is the specific question before Your Honour right at this moment, not these broader issues raised by Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if such be the case, then the argument just posed by Mr. Saxon and I responded to is irrelevant, and I do apologise for taking up the Court's time in that regard. The fact of the matter is that I think it's very clear that this type of evidence is evidence which is a new document for purposes of the analysis that we're engaged in here, and, as such, falls within the jurisprudence. And -- I mean, I think it's of importance - excuse me, I have to find something - that in the self-same paragraph that Mr. Saxon is reading from, that's paragraph 15, and relying on, it says: "The Appeals Chamber" -- The last sentence: "The Appeals Chamber further clarifies that in this decision the term is not limited to the material that was not available to the Prosecution during its case in chief." Well, what information was available to the Prosecution during its case in chief? Obviously, if none other information, most assuredly the information that was contained on their 65 ter list. That's why I'm suggesting the disjunctive as opposed to -- the disjunctive as opposed to conjunctive reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber does not feel fully prepared to rule on this objection at this stage. The Chamber would like to study the situation a little further. Is it possible, Mr. Saxon, that you can deal with other documents which are not fresh evidence - I'm just using that word colloquially, not legally - so that the Chamber can find time to think about this and study the totality of this. We'll try to do it while the witness is here. To the extent that the Defence would say they have had sufficient notice, those are all issues, of course, that will have to be taken into account. We'll try to do it while he's here, and we'll see what happens, if we hear any further arguments on sufficient time and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could change the order of my examination-in-chief. Just to warn the Court as to what is coming, after this document that we've been discussing the last few minutes was dealt with, I had intended to show the witness another exhibit, a Prosecution exhibit, again related to the Drina Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it an exhibit or is it a --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is an exhibit, it is an admitted exhibit, Your Honour. But then at that stage I was planning on having this particular discussion that we've just begun on the issue of fresh evidence, because the Prosecution has a series of documents, similar to what I've been showing to this witness, related to the Army of Republika Srpska's work on the Drina Plan that were never put on the Prosecution's 65 ter list, nor, obviously, admitted into evidence. And so the discussion at that point, in other words, just one or two documents from now, I was planning on having a broader discussion as to why the Prosecution wishes to use these documents at this time with this witness; that the Prosecution, again, because we were told about this defence -- line of defence on Wednesday, we then found these documents, and we would like to use them with the witness to test his credibility. We haven't decided -- and I've got about a dozen documents from the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS, and a similar number of documents from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps of the VRS, and a similar number of documents from the Drina Corps of the VRS; and what the Prosecution was hoping to do today was to use these documents with the witness to test his evidence, mark them for identification, and decide -- and perhaps have a final discussion as to whether they may be admitted into evidence as inculpatory evidence after the witness's testimony is done, after all cross-examination, Judges' questions, and redirect. That was going to be the Prosecution's proposal today, Your Honour, hoping to do this in a reasonably efficient way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, of the 178 documents that we received from the Prosecution and that they indicated they might be using cross-examination, I think that they have identified now somewhere in the neighbourhood of 40, give or take a few - I'm using your figures of 12, 12, and 12, which I think comes to 36, plus I know that you have another couple of 65 ter documents that I think fall in the same category of discussion - I don't know whether or not there's going to be any examination with regard to the other exhibits, the actual P exhibits or D exhibits, which may be a matter to allow the Chamber time to reflect further on the general issue, although Mr. Saxon obviously is not only free but obviously going to do his cross-examination in any fashion he deems appropriate, but it seems to me that, first of all, as a practical matter, there may be a way of dealing with those exhibits that you wish to cross-examine Mr. Simic about that are, in fact, not in dispute with regard to this particular issue. I offer that as a first thought. I think that the Chamber's aware of the fact that, when dealing with this kind of evidence and this kind of proffer, that the analysis is on an ad-hoc basis, which would mean, literally, document by document, which could be quite tedious and cumbersome in the absence of us all having some common ground and familiarity with the underlying jurisprudence. So I don't believe that Mr. Saxon's suggestion, although I understand what it is, I don't think it's terribly practical at the moment. But, then again, I don't know what other areas of examination he intended to go into. And perhaps I'll pass the floor back to him to deal with that to see whether or not there's a way of accommodating the Chamber's question in the first instance or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From what I understand Mr. Saxon to be saying, it seems as if, indeed, he is not in the position to accommodate the Chamber, because two documents from now he would be getting into this same area, with a difference that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He may have another topic, is what I was suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- with a difference that that time the documents are not on the 65 ter list and therefore they take a slightly different shade. But, again, a decision would have to be made at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I agree. And what I was suggesting, and perhaps I -- Mr. Saxon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it would suit the Chamber, I can -- I will take my cross-examination out of order, at least until the end of this session, if that suits the Chamber. And I will deal with documents that have been admitted, if that is -- I just wanted to foreshadow what was coming today, that's all, before a final decision was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Shall we recall the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court is indebted to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I feel it to be my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to take some time to explore with you the subject of sanctions that were imposed on the Republika Srpska by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, starting in August of 1994. And I believe you'll recall that this included a blockade of the Drina River so that goods, with the exception of humanitarian aid, could not pass from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia across the river to the Republika Srpska. Have I described that reasonably well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on Tuesday of this week, at page 9996, lines 11 through 18, you testified that the VJ, and I'm quoting now, "fully" honoured the decision of the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia concerning the sanctions imposed on the -- on Republika Srpska. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness -- first of all, the witness needs to be given his binder that refers -- excuse me. Now, I have a document for the witness. Mr. Usher, if you could come over here. Could we bring up on e-court Prosecution Exhibit P222. I have a copy in the witness's language. If you could show this to Mr. Lukic so that he's all right with providing it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Simic, you'll see that this is an article from the "Borba" daily newspaper, dated Friday, 5th of August, 1994, and it's titled "Federal Government Decides to Cut Political and Economic Ties with Republika Srpska." And then it says: "Border on the Drina Closed." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there's a discussion in the early paragraphs about the decision of the Government of the FRY to cut all political and economic ties with Republika Srpska. And then in the English version, about two-thirds of the way down the page, there's a stand-alone sentence that says: "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia border is closed for all shipments into Republika Srpska except food, clothes, and medicine." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we -- if this article was published on the 5th of August, 1994, can we -- can we agree that the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia made its decision to begin imposing sanctions on the 4th of August? Can we agree on that? Mr. Simic, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. Prosecutor. Just give me a minute to look at it and to refresh my memory. I see that this article is dated the 5th of August. It seems to me, but I'm not quite sure, I think that the sanctions came into force on the 8th of August. That's what I think. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. We can move away from this exhibit now. And I believe now if we could give the witness his binder with the Prosecution exhibit documents, P documents, and if we could call up Exhibit -- and if we could call up Exhibit P230 on e-court, please. And there should be a tab -- and maybe the usher might still be able to assist the witness, because there are many tabs. We're looking for the tab that says "P230."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I was under the impression that the documents were put in the order that you were going to put questions to me. Therefore, I'm finding it a bit difficult to find my bearings, but I will do my best to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I completely understand, and I'm very grateful for your patience. When we come back to a different topic, you will see that the documents that I show you, if I'm allowed to show them to you, are in a particular order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you take a look at this document, which is Exhibit P230, you'll see it says "Defence, State Secret" at the top, and it's a record of a meeting of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska representatives of the highest political and military leadership held on the 25th of August, 1995, at the Army of Yugoslavia Residence in Dobanovci. You see that at the top on the first page?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we'll see -- in the third paragraph, we see who was present from the Yugoslav side; President Zoran Lilic, Slobodan Milosevic, Momir Bulatovic, Radoje Kontic, Lieutenant-General Momcilo Perisic, Federal Minister of Defence Pavle Bulatovic, Major-General Susic. And then we see in the next paragraph the members of the delegation from the Republika Srpska, which included Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Lieutenant General Mladic, et cetera. And then in the fourth paragraph - I'm still on the first page, General Simic - it says: "The meeting was also attended by His Holiness Pavle, the Patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church, and by the Orthodox Bishop Irinej Bulovic." Do you see that, General Simic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And now I'd like to take you to what is -- at least on the hard copy, it's page 14 in the Serbo-Croat version. So if you could turn -- the page numbers are in the upper right-hand corner, General. So if you turn to page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for those following along in English, if we could go to page 11 of the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you please focus, General, on the end of the top paragraph on page 14. There's -- the penultimate sentence begins with the name "Bishop Irinej." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that sentence and the last sentence says the following: "Bishop Irinej advocated the tacit lifting of the Drina River blockade. President Milosevic responded that the blockade was merely a formality and that aid flows daily." Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, given the fact that -- given the persons who were in attendance at that meeting, including General Perisic, that would be an indication that members of the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the army perhaps were not so serious, in terms of their decision to enforce the blockade, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's not fair to put the question to the witness in this way, because he hasn't seen the entire document. He's being asked to comment on one single sentence. The witness needs to know the whole content of the document, and he needs to be familiar with the context. In order for the witness to answer this question, he needs to familiarise himself with the entire content of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if that is the standard, then any time we have a document that is more than a page or two long, and there are many such documents in this case, this will be a very long trial indeed. The context of the -- if you'll forgive me, Counsel, and let me finish. These two sentences, we see a single exchange between the bishop and President Milosevic. The bishop makes a comment; President Milosevic responds to the comment. What more context is needed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand -- or I would understand had the witness been in attendance of this meeting, and in that case he would have been able to answer Mr. Saxon's questions. But to extract a single sentence from a document and ask the witness about it will be misleading for the Chamber as well. He may only guess on the basis of one sentence alone, and, therefore, his answer might not be reliable. I'm not going to testify, but in order for the witness to give a reply to Mr. Saxon's question, he needs to know what the topic of the whole debate was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were many topics discussed in this meeting. I asked the witness -- the witness testified, Your Honour, that the Army of Yugoslavia fully complied with the decision of the Federal Government of Yugoslavia to set up a blockade along the Drina River. And I'm asking the witness to comment, to see if he will agree with the argument that I am making, or not, as to whether this exchange indicates whether this was a serious blockade or not. And my question was at page 19, line 6 to 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think that your objection has a basis, Mr. Lukic. Secondly, I do think that even if it may, this witness can give any answer that he wants to give. He either agrees, disagrees, doesn't know, cannot comment, you know, because he was not -- there are any number of answers that he can give, and he can tell us whether he's able to answer or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: As I recall Mr. Lukic yesterday asking questions of the witness, and you said, I don't want a professional question, I just want an opinion, you know. And so I think that the Prosecution are always asking for an opinion of the witness in relation to this issue, so that was the argument you used yesterday in asking the witness for an opinion. At the objection of the Prosecution that he was not an expert, you said, Well, I am not asking this matter as an excerpt, I am asking as an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge David, Your Honour, you have quoted me precisely, but we are talking about two different things here. I sought his opinion based on the information that he has in his mind about certain facts. Now Mr. Saxon is asking him to express and offer his position on the basis of a single sentence extracted from a document. The Trial Chamber will not have any assistance from this witness unless he is fully familiar with the whole document. And I also disagree with Mr. Saxon that various subjects were discussed at this meeting. There was only one topic on the agenda of this meeting, and Mr. Saxon knows that very well. And I think that things are a little bit distorted -- maybe not distorted, but, Your Honours, you're not going to get a useful testimony from this witness unless he knows what was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking this witness to comment on something that I have just told him about, something that is now part of his knowledge, and that is the content of a portion of a contemporaneous document in which many subjects related to the armed conflict that was going on in Republika Srpska were discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat my question, General Simic, because it's been a while since I've asked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Bishop Ir inej advocated the tacit lifting of the Drina River blockade. President Milosevic responded that the blockade was merely a formality and that aid flows daily. Wouldn't that indicate that this so-called blockade wasn't being taken very seriously by the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, first of all, I cannot comment on any political decision. Secondly, in my previous statements, I said that the army, within its zones of responsibility, honoured this decision. Please bear in mind that I said that the Customs Service and the border crossings were not under the jurisdiction of the army, and Mr. Perisic was not in charge of that, as for what happened in this meeting, because yours truly didn't have an opportunity to attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Simic, you haven't answered my question. I'm not asking you to comment on any political decision. I'm asking you to respond to a question that I put to you based on a portion of this record of this meeting, and I'd like an answer to my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Mr. Simic answered on page 22, line 14, and that he provided a comprehensive answer to the Prosecutor's question. The line reference is 14 to 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness did not answer my question. My question was not about what the Customs Service was doing. My question was: Didn't this comment by President Milosevic indicate that the Government of the FRY didn't treat this as a very serious blockade? And I'd like an answer to my question. It can be a Yes, or a No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said on page 22, line 14: [In English] "First of all, I cannot comment on any political decisions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I have answered. Mr. Prosecutor, as for Customs, the border crossings were secured by the forces of the MUP, and aid convoys, if you insist on that, could not go through the mountains or field paths, in other words, through the areas for which the VJ was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In response to what you just told us, General Simic, it's at least possible -- it was at least possible, wasn't it, for aid to move through the 100-metre zone along the border that was under the responsibility of the Army of Yugoslavia, wasn't it? Wasn't that at least possible?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if you're alluding to some aid, aid cannot be carried in a backpack by an illegal transporter. It has to go on large trucks which can only use legal crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There were pontoon bridges and ferries that were available to be set up to take materials across the Drina River during the armed conflict; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ferries, actually, not pontoon bridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. Can we please call up what is called Exhibit P628. And perhaps the usher could help General Simic find tab 628.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, General Simic, a short time ago you said that, to your recollection, the blockade of goods along the Drina River went into effect on the 8th of August, 1994. This is a document where the date at the top is not fully legible. It says "15 August 19," and it's difficult to read the next two numbers. But if you look towards the bottom, you'll see a receipt stamp from the Special Unit Corps of the Army of Yugoslavia dated the 17th of August, 1994. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see both.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is a -- this is a document signed by General Perisic, then the Chief of the General Staff, and General Perisic says that pursuant to an order of the president of the FRY, dated the 18th of February of that year --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps -- no, we're all right in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "... I issued instruction for the replenishment of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading this from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's right at the top of the English version on the ELMO, Your Honour: "... I issued an instruction for replenishment" -- Could we scroll up a bit on -- could we move up a bit so we -- now I think you can see the whole document, Your Honour. "Pursuant to an order of the president dated 18 February 1994, I issued an instruction ..." Do you see that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "... which was submitted to you under a highly-confidential number," there's a number, "dated February 22, 1994." And then, General Simic, it says the following: "Despite constant warnings, certain commanding officers of the Army of Yugoslavia disobeyed the order and issued equipment for the needs of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centre without authorisation. Disciplinary and criminal procedures are under way for the responsible individuals." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then it says, in relation to this: "1. Warn all those issuing orders and material organs to strictly implement the measures and procedures from the mentioned instruction." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, nowhere -- now, material for the 30th and 40th Personnel Centre meant material to the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of -- the Serbian Army of Krajina, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you look at this document, General Simic, you'll see that about a week after the blockade was imposed, General Perisic is not saying, Stop providing material to the Army of Republika Srpska. He's not saying that. He's saying, Do this according to my previous instructions. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you see, the blockade had been imposed about a week before General Perisic sent this document, and you testified that the Army of Yugoslavia fully complied with the decision of the Government of the FRY. And in this document, General Perisic is saying, If you're going to give materials to the Army of Republika Srpska, do it according to my instructions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, Mr. Prosecutor, and there was no need for him to repeat what he had operationalised in more detail in that instruction. That is why he -- here he didn't use the term you're insisting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to move on from that document now. If we could bring up on the screen Exhibit P851. And hopefully you have a tab that says "851," General. If not, I have a copy of the document in your language. But it should be there. We'll wait for the e-court version to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you'll see this is a document from the Office of the Chief of the VJ General Staff -- I'm sorry, we'll wait. It's tab 851, please. General, this is a document from the Office of the Chief of the General Staff, dated the 22nd of February, 1995, to the commander of the Republika Srpska Army Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And perhaps now to assist those following in English on the -- if we could increase the bottom half of the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you'll see it starts off: "Ratko. "In mid-September 1994, the Supreme Council had made a decision to suspend payment of salaries to your people. After that, we have agreed that I send you 500.000 dinars, which I did on 21 September. The money was collected by General Tomic." And then, below that, General Perisic is asking for some documentation regarding who from the VRS received the payment. Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Wouldn't this 500.000-dinar distribution, if I can call it that, made by General Perisic to the Army of Republika Srpska in mid-September 1994 indicate that the Army of Yugoslavia perhaps was not fully complying with the blockade of the Drina River and of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's something I don't quite understand, Mr. Prosecutor. This document was registered in the Office of the Chief of General Staff on the 22nd of February, 1995, and you are speaking about -- or, rather, we can read in the document that the time-period referred to is 1994. So something is wrong here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Simic, I'm asking you -- my question referred to the content of this document. The first paragraph describes something that occurred in mid-September 1994. It describes something that happened in the past. It describes a payment of 500.000 dinars sent by General Perisic to the Army of Republika Srpska. And my question, I'll ask it again: Wouldn't that indicate that the Army of Yugoslavia was not fully complying with the blockade of the Drina River and of the -- Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, no. If the Trial Chamber will allow me a more detailed explanation, I'm willing to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are in the lawyer's hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Please. Please, Mr. Simic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, once the JNA started pulling out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, both armies were established. Part of the officers who hailed from those areas stayed behind. Some officers pulled out, as members of the VJ, and then those who were born in Republika Srpska or had some other ties with that territory were sent to that army through the 30th or 40th Personnel Centres. Those centres are organisational units of the Personnel Administration of the General Staff. Their purpose was to have a register at one place of all those persons to enable them to claim their status-related rights. Let's not forget that those people who stayed behind, once the two armies were separated, had families in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and, well, they had to make a living.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Earlier today, we looked at what was Prosecution P222, which was the article from "Borba" describing the imposition of the sanctions on Republika Srpska, which said that: "The FRY border is closed for all shipments into Republika Srpska except food, clothes, and medicine." Are you suggesting that money for salaries for army officers falls into the realm of food, clothes, and medicine; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Prosecutor, with all due respect to you, that we are referring to two different periods. At the time when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - in the month of August - when the leadership of the RS refused the contact group's plan, sanctions were imposed on the Drina River, and earlier there had already been the UN sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. Shall we take the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I'm not quite sure whether you want to carry on or you want the Chamber to revisit that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm in the middle of a topic right now, and I need to show the witness some more documents. Perhaps we could finish this topic and then move to the discussion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could call up on e-court, please, Exhibit P1257. And, General Simic, you should have a red tab there that says that, "P1257."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Simic, you'll see this is a document dated the 27th of February, 1995, from the Military Post 2082 in Belgrade, and it says it's signed by Dragoljub Ojdanic. And it says, in the first paragraph: "On the basis of Ruling Confidential Number 85-7 of the 24th of February, 1995, by the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, please issue to the 30th Personnel Centre from Military Post 5292, Mrsac, the following:" And it refers to 150-millimetre contact fuses for a Howitzer cannon and 100 pieces. Are you follow me there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in the penultimate sentence, it says: "The sign-off of the above-stated ammunition is to be done in accordance with the above-stated ruling by the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we -- for the next document, Your Honour, I would ask you to please move into private session, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can call up -- I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Simic, this document is from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated the 19th of June, 1995. It says "Very Urgent" to the General Staff of the VJ, and then to the attention of the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ. Below that, it says "Support and Ammunition," and below that, "Request." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then we see on the -- if we can scroll down, please, in the B/C/S version on e-court for the public. We can see -- and if we go to the next page in the English version, we can see that starting at the bottom of page 1 in B/C/S, we see a list of requested ammunition, and -- which continues on to the second -- on to the third page in the English version, on to the second page in B/C/S. If we go to the next page in B/C/S, please, and could we -- we see that the document is coming from Commander Ratko Mladic. And could we please scroll down in both versions, please. Could we go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see at the bottom there, in the B/C/S version, there's a telegram. Are you with me, General? At the very end of the document, there's a telegram. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, on page 4, on the very last -- excuse me, on page -- on the second page in your version, the bottom of the second page. You'll see a --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I can see, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And that's -- again, that's from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, from the Cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff to the Logistics Sector, to General Milovanovic. Can you read for us, please, then, what that telegram says? Can you read it, please, out loud?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We hereby forward to you the telegram of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and inform you that the Chief of General Staff of the VJ ordered: 'Give it to Ratko to have it sorted out.'" And signed chief of the -- chief -- it only says: "Chief, Colonel Sinisa Borovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted the witness to read it out in the original language, because it indicates that in the last page of the English, there is an error in the English translation. In the second line of the telegram, it says "Chief of the VRS Main Staff." That should be the VJ General Staff, Your Honour. That's what the witness just read into the record. So I just wanted to correct the record for this exhibit. Can we please remove that document now and -- one moment, please. Can we now -- I now have a series of documents -- two documents that need to be viewed in private session. Could we look at P2736, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After we've moved into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After we've moved into private session. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. 23 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if this could not be published to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I'll wait for that. It's not -- here it comes on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you'll see this is a document from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It's dated the 1st of September, 1995. It's marked "Urgent," to the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ. And in the first paragraph, it refers to a confidential letter of the 21st of July, 1995, where: "... we requested the 172nd ssrp to be replenished with three kub-m rocket batteries and reinforced with personnel." And then it says: "We have received only one rocket battery." Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page, please, in English. And if we could scroll to the bottom of the B/C/S page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, again you'll see this came from Colonel General Ratko Mladic, and there's a telegram at the bottom again from the Yugoslav Army General Staff, Office of the Chief of the General Staff, dated the 1st of September, 1995, to the Sector for Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence. Again, could you please read the contents of that telegram out loud, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I do that, Mr. Prosecutor, let me just add one thing. This is not a telegram from the General Staff of the VJ, sent to the RV and PVL Sector, but, rather, his chief of the staff is forwarding the telegram received from the Main Staff of the VRS to his assistant for logistics to study it and to prepare a proposal for the Chief of General Staff. Have I been clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You've been very clear, and thank you for clarifying that for us. Thank you. Could you please read the message that is there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes: "We are forwarding a telegram of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and we kindly ask you to make a proposal to be submitted to the Chief of General Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could stay in private session for a moment longer, and if we could look at Exhibit P2746, please. This is a document that's been admitted under seal. I'm waiting for the English of this document to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, again, this is a request from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated the 7th of October, 1995, again marked "Very Urgent," addressed to the Command of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, Chief of General Staff personally. It says: "Sending 10 FAB-275/4 aerial bomb request." And then in the first paragraph, if you go to what is probably the second page in your version, it says: "Please send us 10 FAB-275/4. Since we do not have any such ammunition and considering the short time available to us, please send the ammunition to the 30th Logistics Base as soon as possible." Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in English, please, and what is probably -- in your version, it's the first page. It may be out of order. I'm not sure. Again, we see a message from the General Staff, Office of the Chief of General Staff, dated the 7th of October, 1995. And, again, this is addressed to the Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence Sector, and it says: "The Chief of the General Staff of the VJ has approved for," it should be, "the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to be resolved as soon as possible. Please send your reply." Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, we'll have to stay in private session for one document more. If we could please see Exhibit P2731. And could we go to the next page in the English version, please, and to the next page in the Serbo-Croat version, please. Okay. And there should be a document in B/C/S dated the 27th of June, 1995. Here we're seeing the document from the 28th of June. I believe there's one more page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's start with the document dated the 27th of June, please. It's from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It's marked "Urgent" to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, addressed to the Chief of the General Staff. And then it says the following: "In Brezovik store, there are 200 'grad' motors, bought for the needs of the VRS, still not taken nor transferred to Republika Srpska." And then it says: "The assistant commander for logistics in the 2nd Army does not approve giving and transferring of motors without your order." "I would like to ask you to make possible giving and transferring to Republika Srpska the above-mentioned quantity of 'grad' motors." And then it's from Colonel-General Ratko Mladic, personally. Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now can we turn to the earlier page in both the English and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This document, dated the 28th of June, 1995, from the Office of the Chief of the General Staff to the Command of the 2nd Army, the assistant commander for logistics, and it says: "In regard to the request of the VRS Main Staff for the giving and transfer to Republika Srpska 200 'grad' motors, hereby we inform you that the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ has ordered all stated assets to be given to the VRS." It's signed for the Chief of Office Colonel Dr. Sinisa Borovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So some action was taken by the Office of the Chief of the General Staff the following day; correct? In other words, the day after General Mladic sent his communication to the VJ General Staff, some action was taken by the Office of the Chief of the General Staff. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We can now move into public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honour wishes to wait until it's possible for the blind to be raised, or would you like me to continue? You would like -- I will continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're trying to give the transcript time to disappear, the transcript that was -- otherwise, the people sitting there will read what was said in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does that mean I should pause for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It means you can carry on, and we'll open the blind a little later, when it has disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. If we could show the witness Exhibit P2787, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told the exhibit is confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Then we'll have to go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move back into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was my error, Your Honour, it was my error. 8 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. When you say confidential, do you mean it's under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, your version of this document is not easy to read, so I'm only going to ask you to look at the beginning of the document. It's from the Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff, dated the 3rd of August, 1995. It's marked "Urgent. Submit to the chief of the VJ General Staff." Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then below that, it says: "Take over of the allocated TMS." And then it says: "A request." And then, below that, it says: "By your decision, Strictly Confidential Number 4361-1, from 30 March 1994, the VRS was allocated the following seven helicopters, which have not yet been taken over:" Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then if we can please go to the next page -- actually, to the last page in the English version, and if we could scroll to the end -- go to the end of the B/C/S version. It should be one more page in B/C/S. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see the last item we looked at was dated the 3rd of August, and now we see the document from the 4th of August, 1995, from the VJ General Staff, Sector for Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence, to be sent to -- and we see a list: The VJ General Staff 608th Logistics Base; the Command of the Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence; the VRS Main Staff; and also to the attention of the Chief of the VJ General Staff. And it says: "Pursuant to the VRS Main Staff request dated the 3rd of August, 1995, we agree that the following VTMS be given to the VRS Main Staff:" And then we see, below that, some acronyms. And the first one is "HN-42." That's a kind of helicopter, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One piece. And then we see "HN-45 - two pieces." That's another kind of helicopter; right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then we see "Ho-42 - 3 pieces." It's another kind of helicopter; right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, finally, one "HT-40," which I assume is also a kind of helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this document is signed by Mirko Vrucinic, general major -- major-general, I should say, for the Sector for The RV and PVO, the Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence. Your Honours, can we now move back into public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, what I want to ask you is: Given the documents that I've been showing to you this afternoon, is it still your position that the Army of Yugoslavia fully complied with the blockade in place to prevent materials going to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about something that was not within my purview and my scope of responsibility. When I said that goods did not cross the border-line that was being secured by the Yugoslav Army, I still stand by what I said. However, if you're claiming that we were providing assistance to the Army of Republika Srpska, that is, without doubt, true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So that, in other words, after the blockade -- the so-called blockade was publicly announced in August of 1994, the Army of Yugoslavia continued to provide assistance to the Army of Republika Srpska? That, I think, is what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the blockade was in place in 1995, not in 1994. At least that's what I heard in the translation of your question, 1994. Everything that you're asking me about with respect to all these documents was not within my scope of responsibility, and nowhere can you see that anything went through my administration, nor is it seen that my administration provided approval or anything else. It went to other organisational units and the heads of these respective organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take this slowly. All right? You said a moment ago - this is at page 41, lines 22 to 25: "When I said that goods did not cross the border-line that was being secured by the Yugoslav Army, I still stand by what I said. However, if you're claiming that we were providing assistance to the Army of Republika Srpska, that is, without doubt, true." And I just want to clarify that. What you're saying is: After the blockade was announced, the Army of Yugoslavia continued to provide assistance to the Army of Republika Srpska? That's just my first clarification. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the documents that we have seen, there is no question about it. It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So are you aware of any other kinds of assistance that the Army of Yugoslavia provided to the Army of Republika Srpska after the blockade was announced, apart from what's been in the documents that I've shown you today?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while ago, I mentioned the personnel centres. These personnel centres served precisely the purpose of solving status-related issues and rights of the personnel who left there. Among other things, part of that package was the 500.000 dinars sent by the Chief of General Staff, which means assistance in providing salaries to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. My fault. My question wasn't clear enough. When I said if you were aware of other kinds of assistance, apart from what we saw in the documents today, I was referring to materiel; materiel, equipment, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not within my department, but I know that there were other assets, what we call equipment used for war. This is one general name for all these assets that are being used to wage war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And what kind of -- can you describe the kinds of assets that you're referring to, these assets that were being used to wage war? Can you give some examples?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these assets include armaments, ammunition, fuel, lubricants, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm finished with this topic now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you handing over to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to -- yes, effectively, yes, in case at this time you wanted to discuss the other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber looked at the -- studied the matter. Obviously, for the Trial Chamber to be able to make a ruling on this issue, the concerns raised in these decisions need to be addressed; the mode of disclosure, the purpose of the document, what is it -- what is it proving, and the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask Mr. Saxon to switch off his mike. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and the time spent when it was delivered, disclosed. You know, all those points need to be addressed before we can make a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, do I take from what Your Honour has just advised us, then, that the Chamber is ruling that a document included on Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit list falls within the universe of what we refer to as fresh evidence? Is that what I take from your ruling, because that's what was subject to -- that's what we were discussing in the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What the Trial Chamber wants to rule on is on whether to allow the Prosecution to use that document or not. And the argument that it is part of the 65 ter list or not will be part of the submissions that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before Mr. Saxon starts, I have one question to ask, which I believe is appropriate, given the Chamber's ruling, which is: It is our assumption that the Prosecution's going to seek to admit whatever we wish to call this body of documents in order to establish the guilt of the accused. I see Mr. Saxon waving his finger at me, so that may not be the case. I think that may be of some import or not with regard to the discussion, but -- so if he could identify, when discussing these documents, which position the Prosecution's taking with them, that also, I think, would be helpful for purposes of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me make it quite clear from the point of view of the Chamber. The Chamber is not talking about the batch of documents. The Chamber is talking about the one document, 65 ter 2022.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay, very well. I'm with you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's a fair point that my colleague is raising, and it may be -- it may be more appropriate, Your Honour, to ask the witness to step out for a minute. I don't know how else -- how else to do this. Then I won't, Your Honour. I see that that's not acceptable to the Chamber. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, I never -- how do you get it that it's not acceptable to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I saw you shaking your head, and I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no. I can shake my head, but I wasn't responding to you. I was actually smiling at Mr. Simic because I was feeling sorry for him. Mr. Simic, I'm sorry, again we are going to ask you to please step out for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution seeks permission to use this document, as well as other documents that were not on its 65 ter list today, related to the Drina Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, let me warn you up front. It's going to have to be looked at on a case-by-case basis. And we're dealing now with one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Well, then the purposes of this document, we want to use it with the witness to carry on impeaching his evidence, Your Honour, not necessarily to admit the document into evidence. What we would like to do is review the document with the witness, get his comments, mark it for identification, and then what we would propose doing, and again with other documents, is to, at the end of this witness's evidence, after all cross-examination, after redirect and the Judges' questions, make any final discussions as to whether these documents might be admitted as inculpatory evidence against the accused. We are seeking permission at this time to use them for purposes of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do not follow you there, Mr. Saxon, that you want to tender the document, use it against the witness for purposes of impeachment, and still reserve the right later to change that purpose into inculpatory evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the their purpose -- this is precisely -- well, let me say my concern is why the purpose would change along the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The purpose that would change would be whether we seek the admission of these documents or not, that -- that is the purpose that would change. What we're asking to do -- to be allowed to do, preliminarily, is use these documents at least for the purposes of impeaching the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let us understand the way "purposes" is used in the Appeals Chamber's decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber's decisions are about the decision whether or not to admit the document. And in order to admit it, the purpose for its being tendered is to be determined. So whether it's going to be admitted or not could not be a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As I've read -- with the greatest respect, Your Honour, is I have read, for example -- as I have read the jurisprudence, Your Honour, there is a high threshold that the Prosecution must show that it is in the interests of justice to tender inculpatory fresh evidence, rather than - and there is a lower standard - than for evidence used solely for impeachment purposes. That's how I'm reading, and that's why I'm making this distinction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear you, and I agree with you on that point. Now, but I'm -- I was still at a lower level, a lower threshold.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And at the lower threshold, there are a number of preconditions that must be addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The mode of disclosure of the document in question, the purpose for their admission, the time lapsed between disclosure and examination of the witness, the language known to counsel and the accused, as well as any other relevant factual considerations. Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then let me -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If, at this stage, then the purpose, which is number 2, the purpose for the admission is to inculpate the accused, then the higher threshold kicks in. However, I do not understand why the purpose can initially be for purposes of impeachment, and then when it is in, then we say, No, no, now we want it to inculpate the accused. You've got to state up front whether you want to inculpate the accused or is it for purposes of impeachment, in which case, then -- in which case, then, if it's to incriminate the accused, then the higher standard kicks in. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we on a wavelength --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We are on a wavelength, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm talking about procedural --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- that the admission could not be a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the purpose of our using the document this time is to impeach the witness. That is our purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you, Mr. Guy-Smith. And that would be the purpose --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- right through the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, we're talking on a case-by-case basis, so I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, and we're dealing with this case -- this case or this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This -- exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that's the purpose of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- right through the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Court's indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, Your Honour, we will -- we seek your permission to use this document for the purposes of impeaching the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a question before you ask for the indulgence. Is that purpose, with respect to this document, is the only purpose for the entirety of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the reason I asked you this question is earlier you accept you might later want to use it to inculpate, you might want to change that purpose for impeaching to inculpate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you're not going to do that with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
